362	As a Rebbe he had a silver bowl, but
363	for our purposes,
364	the poor
365	would bring what they could, in straw baskets. They
366	would of course choose a nice basket,
367	well made. Maybe even, I assume, it's quite

369	the fondness to prepare the basket himself, if he

372	But in the end, a straw basket.
373	Rabbi, there is a fix, somewhere that...
374	Surely, everything I'm saying now, I'm not inventing it.
375	It's all, not in pictures.
376	There were no pictures. We're talking about the last time
377	the mitzvah of Bikurim was fulfilled, about
378	1,960 years ago, in the time of the Second Temple.
379	And there were no photographs yet. There are paintings, but not
380	photographs, nor paintings since then, though paintings could
381	have been made. So today it's possible to draw. No paintings
382	survived from then, to my knowledge at least. Also
383	then there was no paper, so there was nothing to draw on.
384	Now,
385	the novelty was that specifically with the poor,
386	the basket too would remain in the Temple.
387	They would not take it back home. Rather, every year
388	they would bring to the Temple not only the fruits but
389	the holiness would actually penetrate this basket too.
390	It was an advantage of the poor over the rich. With
391	the rich it looked much more beautiful.
392	The picture of the king bringing the Bikurim is not
393	a straw basket, but a basket of gold. But
394	with all due respect, he takes the basket back.
395	Whereas the poor, everything they brought to HaShem,
396	HaShem accepts it all.
397	In any case,
398	every first fruit... Was it a huge quantity?
399	The quantity was enormous, or...
400	The quantity was not enormous, but yes,
401	every first fruit, and it's roughly a ratio of one percent,
402	or a bit more than one percent of all the fruits. But it
403	can end up being a significant basket, yes.
404	Surely in halakhah there is even a definition of the order
405	of the fruits, so that the fruits, for example the grapes, must
406	be on top; if they were at the bottom, of course they would
407	be crushed. Only from the seven species.
408	Only from the seven species. Now,
409	whoever wanted to beautify his basket even more
410	would tie turtledoves and young pigeons to it.
411	Picture to yourselves how that looks: a basket tied
412	to turtledoves and young pigeons, like doves.
413	They were real doves, certainly, which they bring
414	as an offering to HaShem, those...
415	Yes, they would do it in a way that would not harm them.
416	Now, in any case, what is the point? The point is
417	that merely mentioning this mitzvah
418	already fills us with a feeling of joy
419	and warmth, because it is truly an extraordinary mitzvah.
420	We have no example. What is the closest example
421	to this mitzvah today, in terms of the heartfelt emotion that accompanies
422	this mitzvah, and the preparation, and the guidance, and the connection,
423	the feeling of connection to HaShem, the closest we have?
424	That is actually the experience of the Seder night, with all
425	the preparations made for the Seder, with all the splendor on
426	the Seder table, with the Haggadah. And why do I say
427	the Haggadah? Because it is actually the climax, it is what
428	we began to say earlier, the climax.
429	For a whole group came, sometimes dozens or
430	perhaps hundreds of Jews, each one coming with his basket of
431	Bikurim on that same day, in that same
432	procession,
433	and
434	each one places his basket. But it does not
435	end there; each one waits for his turn.
436	And when
437	the turn arrives, as it is written in the Scroll of Esther, "when the turn of the maiden arrived,"
438	the turn of the specific
439	person who brought his basket of Bikurim.
440	Then he recites the Bikurim declaration, which is detailed
441	in the Parashah: "And you shall speak and say before HaShem your Elokim."
442	And the Jew recites the Bikurim declaration with feeling,
443	with joy,
444	with tremendous excitement.
445	And who is listening to him? Everyone. That is, at that moment
446	he is at the center of attention, and everyone, all the Kohanim,
447	surround him, everyone is listening to him, all
448	the Jews who came with him, everyone listens. One at a time.
449	Each one gets all the space, all the...
450	This reminds me of something, in a total aside,
451	some experience where each person gets the
452	most exalted privilege.
453	With the Rebbe. What is there with the Rebbe in this matter?
454	Not that the Rebbe gives everyone a dollar or a lekach or
455	a blessing; that gaze of the Rebbe on you for two
456	seconds is something very, very special, but
457	in the end it is something the Rebbe gives you. It is from the Rebbe. It is
458	no novelty that the Rebbe gives every Jew the feeling
459	that he is a king, that he is the most important thing,
460	the most precious to him, because that is truly how it is,
461	in those seconds.
462	In those seconds. But there is something closer to
463	what we are describing now, which is a once-in-a-lifetime privilege
464	and is the privilege of grooms.
465	Every groom, before his wedding day, has one
466	single opportunity: the Rebbe gives him his personal siddur
467	to pray the Mincha prayer with it.
468	So think what an excitement it is to stand
469	and receive the Rebbe's siddur.
470	In the times when we merited to see the Rebbe, it was receiving
471	the siddur from the Rebbe's holy hands. Not every
472	one would receive it, because if there were several
473	grooms, the Rebbe would ask who is older, or who is a Kohen,
474	or who... He would not give it, and they would pass it from one
475	to another. But in the end each one stands for the duration of
476	the Mincha prayer, which can be a significant time,
477	and prays from the Rebbe's siddur, and of course it is
478	the prayer in which you ask for everything you want to ask
479	for your whole life, not only for yourself, for the bride too.
